title: Classify a triangle by both sides and angles, in any orientation

lesson.title: Naming a Triangle Two Ways — No Matter How It Sits

steps.say: You already know how to name a triangle by its sides — scalene, isosceles, equilateral — and by its angles — right, acute, obtuse. Today we do just one small new thing: give a triangle both names at once, and keep that name even when the triangle is tipped, flipped, or lying on its side.

visual.caption: One triangle, two questions: what about its sides? what about its angles?

steps.say: Here is the whole trick. Ask two questions in order. First, sides: are all three the same, are two the same, or are they all different? Second, angles: is there a square corner, a corner bigger than a square corner, or are all three corners small? Then say the side word first and the angle word second, like an isosceles right triangle. Two questions, two words, one name.

Let us try a real one. Imagine a cedar shelf bracket from the hardware store in Burnaby. Two of its sides are both six centimetres long, and the corner between them is a perfect square corner, ninety degrees. The other two corners are forty five degrees each. Check: forty five plus forty five plus ninety makes one hundred and eighty. Sides first — two sides match, so it is isosceles. Angles next — there is a ninety degree corner, so it is right. Its full name is an isosceles right triangle.

visual.caption: The square corner: ninety degrees means right triangle.

steps.say: Now the mistake I see all the time. I screw that same bracket onto the wall upside down, with the square corner pointing up instead of down. A lot of kids look at it and say, that is not a right triangle any more! But nothing changed. The two sides are still six centimetres and six centimetres. The corner is still ninety degrees. Turning a triangle is like turning your lunch container — the sandwich inside is exactly the same. So it is still an isosceles right triangle.

visual.caption: Same bracket, turned around. Same lengths, same angles, same name.

steps.say: So remember: measure, do not eyeball. Sides first, angles second, and never let the way it is sitting on the page fool you.

lesson.answer: Name it twice — sides first, angles second — and turning the triangle never changes its name.

practice.question: A metal bracket on a fence in Kamloops is shaped like a triangle. Two of its sides are 5 centimetres and 5 centimetres, and the third side is 8 centimetres. Its biggest angle measures about 106 degrees, and the other two are about 37 degrees each. The bracket is bolted on sideways, so the long 8 centimetre side is standing straight up. Draw it yourself if it helps. What is its full two-word name?
practice.answer: An obtuse isosceles triangle. Two sides match (5 cm and 5 cm), so it is isosceles, and 106 degrees is bigger than a square corner, so it is obtuse. Being bolted on sideways changes nothing — and check the angles: 106 plus 37 plus 37 equals 180.
